newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya says auctions staying, payments to be streamlined.
newsitem.headline: Kenya says auctions staying, payments to be streamlined.

text.p: Kenya's agriculture minister says coffee weekly export auctions will remain but authorities were seeking ways to end delays in payments to farmers.
But Simeon Nyachae told reporters on Tuesday that farmers were hurt by a rising cost in inputs such as fertilisers and this was likely to be reflected in production in the near term.
Nyachae said the government and the marketing agency Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) were in full agreement on coffee reforms and their pace and "we believe we are proceeding very well".
Nyachae said coffee auctions were highly favoured by both farmers and traders and represented the best return to growers.
He confirmed that he had called in coffee board officials to discuss the pressing question of speeding up payments to farmers once the coffee was sold at the auctions, normally in Nairobi.
Nyachae said growers remained discouraged by slow payments and lack of financing for the improvement of their farms.

"We are trying to sort out the credit system to farmers so they can have access to money for inputs such as fertilisers and other chemicals," Nyachae said. "We are also looking at a faster system of releasing money to farmers after auctions."

"The high prices of inputs and services have been a major constraint in production. The high prices prevailing in the early 1990s discouraged many farmers and led to a decline in use of inputs," Nyachae said.

Currently, the coffee board offers coffee for auction and them remits the earnings to coffee factories or cooperatives to onpass to farmers. Factory and cooperative leaders then hold on to the money and decide when the farmers should get it.
Sometimes such a wait extends to four or five months.
"We would like a system where the farmers can get their money at least two weeks after the auction," Nyachae said.
Nyachae also said management company Price Waterhouse had been asked to conduct a coffee industry survey for the European Union on the liberalisation process.

He said such an independent industry audit was important because the European Union, under provisions of the Lome Convention, released money from its STABEX funds to Kenya as compensation when the country's commodity export earnings dropped.
"The Price Waterhouse probe will help the European Union understand our liberalisation process," Nyachae said.
Switzerland-based traders Edm. Schluter & Co Ltd have revised their estimates of 1996/97 production to 90,000 tonnes from a previous 100,000 tonnes owing to a rise in coffee berry disease.

The Coffee Board of Kenya has said it is too early to make an estimate taking into account any disease threat but it had already revised its own 1996/97 predictions. The board first talked of 100,000 tonnes, then revised the figure to 96,000 and currently forecasts output of 95,000 tonnes.
